SafeDream: Safety World Model for Proactive Early Jailbreak Detection

Bo Yan Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: bo949643@ucf.edu    Weikai Lin Affiliation: University of Rochester Email: wlin33@ur.rochester.edu    Yada Zhu Affiliation: IBM Research Email: yzhu@us.ibm.com    Song Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: song.wang@ucf.edu
Abstract

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks progressively erode LLM safety alignment across seemingly innocuous conversation turns, achieving success rates exceeding 90% against state-of-the-art models. Existing alignment-based and guardrail methods suffer from three key limitations: they require costly weight modification, evaluate each turn independently without modeling cumulative safety erosion, and detect attacks only after harmful content has been generated. To address these limitations, we first formulate the proactive early jailbreak detection problem with a new metric, detection lead, that measures how early an attack can be detected before the LLM complies. We then propose SafeDream, a lightweight world-model-based framework that operates as an external module without modifying the LLM’s weights. SafeDream introduces three components: (1) a safety state world model that encodes LLM hidden states into a compact safety representation and predicts how it evolves across turns, (2) CUSUM detection that accumulates weak per-turn risk signals into reliable evidence, and (3) contrastive imagination that simultaneously rolls out attack and benign futures in latent space to issue early alarms before jailbreaks occur. On three multi-turn jailbreak benchmarks (XGuard-Train, SafeDialBench, SafeMTData) against 8 baselines, SafeDream achieves the best detection timeliness across all benchmarks (1.06–1.20 turns before compliance) while maintaining competitive false positive rates and outperforming baselines in detection quality.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) (Yang et al., 2024) can be exploited for harmful purposes such as generating misinformation or illegal instructions. Despite safety mechanisms like alignment training and guardrails (Inan et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024), multi-turn jailbreak attacks remain highly effective (Mazeika et al., 2024): by spreading malicious intent across seemingly innocuous turns, they gradually erode LLM safety barriers until the model complies. Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2025) achieves a 98% binary success rate against GPT-4, FITD (Weng et al., 2025) averages 94% Attack Success Rate (ASR) across seven LLMs, and STAR (Li et al., 2026) reaches 94.5% Safety Failure Rate (SFR) against GPT-4o.

Recent work has explored various approaches to counter jailbreak attempts. Alignment-based methods such as Circuit Breaker (Zou et al., 2024), X-Boundary (Lu et al., 2025), and TARS (Kim et al., 2025) modify LLM weights to resist attacks. Guardrail methods such as WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) and GuardReasoner (Liu et al., 2025) deploy external classifiers to evaluate each turn independently. However, these approaches suffer from three key limitations. First, alignment-based methods require access to and modification of model weights, incurring significant computational overhead and precluding deployment on closed-source models. Second, both paradigms typically evaluate each turn independently, making them unable to defend against multi-turn attacks where the LLM complies only after a gradual safety erosion accumulated across multiple turns. Third, neither paradigm formulates the problem of anticipating jailbreaks before they succeed; by the time these methods detect an attack signal, the LLM may have already generated harmful content.

To address these three limitations, we reformulate the multi-turn jailbreak detection problem (Section 2). Unlike previous formulations, we explicitly incorporate detection lead time, measuring how many turns earlier a jailbreak attempt can be detected before the LLM actually complies. We then propose SafeDream, a world-model-based safety module that enables proactive, early jailbreak detection in multi-turn dialogues. SafeDream addresses the three limitations above: it operates as a lightweight external module without modifying the LLM’s weights (solving limitation 1); it models safety state dynamics across turns rather than evaluating each turn independently (solving limitation 2); and it proactively detects attacks before the LLM complies through contrastive imagination (solving limitation 3).

SafeDream consists of three key components. First, we introduce a Safety State World Model: a lightweight Transformer that predicts future safety states from the safety state history and user actions, operating entirely in a low-dimensional safety state space (Section 3.1). Second, we employ Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) detection to aggregate risk signals across multiple turns, demonstrating how multi-turn safety erosion can be effectively captured through sequential evidence accumulation (Section 3.2). Third, in ambiguous situations, in order to detect jailbreaks as early as possible, we use our Safety State World Model to conduct contrastive imagination, which rolls out possible attack and benign futures and enables early alarms before a jailbreak actually occurs (Section 3.3).

We evaluate SafeDream on three multi-turn jailbreak benchmarks (XGuard-Train (Rahman et al., 2025), SafeDialBench (Cao et al., 2025), SafeMTData (Ren et al., 2025)) against 8 baselines. Our key contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate the proactive early jailbreak detection problem with a new metric, detection lead, that measures how early attacks can be detected before the LLM complies.

  • •

    We propose SafeDream, a world-model-based framework consisting of a safety state world model, CUSUM detection, and contrastive imagination for proactive early jailbreak detection.

  • •

    SafeDream achieves the best detection lead across all benchmarks (1.06–1.20 turns before compliance) and the highest detection quality with only an external module, even outperforming baselines that modify LLM weights.

  • •

    Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our design: contrastive imagination is the primary driver of early detection and CUSUM is the key for false alarm suppression.

2 Problem Formulation

Multi-turn dialogue and safety model.

We study jailbreak detection given an ongoing dialogue between a user and an LLM, the goal is to decide whether the user is steering the conversation toward harmful content before the LLM complies. At turn tt, the user sends utterance utu_{t} and the LLM generates response yty_{t}. We define the observation ot=(u1,y1,…,yt−1,ut)o_{t}=(u_{1},y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1},u_{t}) as the conversation prefix immediately before yty_{t} is generated. A safety model f⁡(ot)∈{0,1}f(o_{t})\in\{0,1\} infers whether jailbreak intent is present; if f⁡(ot)=1f(o_{t})=1, the LLM refuses to respond.

Attack model and compliance point.

In a multi-turn jailbreak, an adversarial user progressively guides the LLM toward harmful content through seemingly innocuous messages, gradually eroding the LLM’s safety alignment until the model fully complies. We call this critical point the compliance point cc, formally defined as the first turn at which the majority of independent safety classifiers flag the LLM’s response as harmful (see Section 3.4 for the labeling procedure). Detecting the attack after the compliance point (t>ct>c) is too late, as harmful content has been generated.

Proactive early jailbreak detection.

Previous defenses show little concern for how early an attack can be detected: guardrails (Han et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) flag harmful content only after it appears, and alignment-based methods (Zou et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025) resist attacks but do not anticipate compliance. We formulate the proactive early jailbreak detection problem: the safety model ff predicts whether the dialogue will eventually reach a compliance point, and we measure timeliness via the detection lead:

Lead=c−tdet,where ​tdet=min⁡{t:f⁡(ot)=1}.\text{Lead}=c-t^{\text{det}},\quad\text{where }t^{\text{det}}=\min\{t:f(o_{t})=1\}. (1)

Here, tdett^{\text{det}} is the earliest turn when the model detects a risk. Positive Lead (tdet<ct^{\text{det}}<c) achieves proactive early detection; negative Lead indicates reactive post-hoc detection. The objective is to maximize Lead while maintaining a low false positive rate on benign conversations.

3 SafeDream: Proactive World Model for Early Jailbreak Detection

We present SafeDream, a world-model-based framework for proactive early jailbreak detection (Fig. 2). The framework introduces a safety state world model (Section 3.1) that encodes the LLM’s hidden state into compact latent safety states and learns to predict future safety states. To reliably detect jailbreak, we employ cumulative sum detection (Section 3.2), which aggregates weak per-turn risk signals into robust statistical evidence. Building on the world model and cumulative detection, we propose contrastive imagination (Section 3.3), which simultaneously predicts attack and benign future roll-outs to quantify vulnerability, enabling proactive early attack detection. We describe the training procedure in Section 3.4.

3.1 Safety State World Model

Proactive early detection requires the ability to predict future safety outcomes from the current state. To this end, we design a world model over safety states, consisting of two components: (1) a safety state extractor eϕe_{\phi} that compresses each turn into a low-dimensional safety state vector 𝐳t=eϕ​(ot)\mathbf{z}_{t}=e_{\phi}(o_{t}), capturing the safety-relevant information of that turn; and (2) a transition model gθg_{\theta} that integrates safety states from previous turns and predicts future safety states based on user actions 𝐚t=ψ⁡(ut)\mathbf{a}_{t}=\psi(u_{t}). Each safety state is converted to risk score by a discriminator dω​(𝐳t)→rt∈[0,1]d_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t})\to r_{t}\in[0,1], where a value of 1 indicates likely jailbreak compliance.

Safety state extraction.

At each turn tt, we feed the conversation prefix oto_{t} through the frozen Qwen2.5-7B (Yang et al., 2024) and extract the hidden state 𝐡t∈ℝ3584\mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3584} from layer 19, which Wollschläger et al. (2025) identify as the layer most strongly associated with safety-related refusal behavior in Qwen-family models. To extract safety-relevant information, we project 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t} onto K=5K{=}5 safety-related directions on the concept cone (Wollschläger et al., 2025), yielding a safety signature 𝐬t∈ℝ5\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{5}. We further enrich 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} via Perceiver-style cross-attention (Jaegle et al., 2022) that uses 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} as queries into 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t}, producing a learned 64-dimensional extension. The final safety state is:

𝐳t=[𝐬t;XAttnϕ​(𝐬t,𝐡t)]∈ℝ69,\mathbf{z}_{t}=[\mathbf{s}_{t}\;;\;\text{XAttn}_{\phi}(\mathbf{s}_{t},\mathbf{h}_{t})]\in\mathbb{R}^{69}, (2)

where the first 5 dimensions are frozen cone projections and the remaining 64 are learned enhancement through ϕ\phi. Architectural details are in Appendix A.2.

Transition model.

The user action 𝐚t=ψ⁡(ut)\mathbf{a}_{t}=\psi(u_{t}) is encoded by embedding the utterance utu_{t} with the frozen LLM, mean-pooling over token embeddings, and linearly projecting the result to a 64-dimensional vector. A causal Transformer gθg_{\theta} then models the safety-state dynamics (Hafner et al., 2025). The goal of the transition model is to predict the next safety state from the current state and user action: given the input token [𝐳t−1;𝐚t][\mathbf{z}_{t-1};\mathbf{a}_{t}], the model outputs the predicted 𝐳^t\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}:

𝐳^t=gθ​((𝐳0,𝐚1),(𝐳1,𝐚2),…,(𝐳t−1,𝐚t)),\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=g_{\theta}\big((\mathbf{z}_{0},\mathbf{a}_{1}),(\mathbf{z}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}),\ldots,(\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\mathbf{a}_{t})\big), (3)

where 𝐳0=𝟎\mathbf{z}_{0}=\mathbf{0} is a fixed initial state. The Transformer has only 1.2M parameters (0.017% of the 7B LLM), enabling the imagination module to roll out futures with negligible overhead.

Safety discriminator.

A two-layer MLP dω​(𝐳t)→rt∈[0,1]d_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t})\to r_{t}\in[0,1] maps each safety state to a risk score, which is used by the cumulative detection module (Section 3.2) and the contrastive imagination module (Section 3.3).

3.2 Cumulative Sum Attack Detection

In a multi-turn attack, the risk score from any single turn is weak and noisy. However, if we accumulate risk signals across turns, genuine attacks reveal a systematic risk increasing trend that distinguishes them from fluctuations in benign conversations. We adopt CUSUM (Page, 1954), a sequential change-point detection method that is provably optimal for minimizing detection delay at a given false alarm rate (Moustakides, 1986).

We first convert each risk score to log-odds via a clipped logit transformation:

Λt=logitϵ​(rt)≜log⁡clip⁡(rt,ϵ, 1−ϵ)1−clip⁡(rt,ϵ, 1−ϵ),\Lambda_{t}=\mathrm{logit}_{\epsilon}(r_{t})\;\triangleq\;\log\frac{\mathrm{clip}(r_{t},\,\epsilon,\,1{-}\epsilon)}{1-\mathrm{clip}(r_{t},\,\epsilon,\,1{-}\epsilon)}, (4)

with ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. The CUSUM statistic accumulates evidence by subtracting a baseline κ\kappa (the average log-odds under benign conversations):

Gt=max⁡(0,Gt−1+Λt−κ),G0=0.G_{t}=\max(0,\;G_{t-1}+\Lambda_{t}-\kappa),\quad G_{0}=0. (5)

In benign conversations, Λt≈κ\Lambda_{t}\approx\kappa and GtG_{t} stays near zero. During an attack, Λt\Lambda_{t} consistently exceeds κ\kappa, causing GtG_{t} to climb steadily. An alarm is raised when Gt≥AG_{t}\geq A.

We define a gray zone (τ​A<Gt<A\tau A<G_{t}<A, τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1)) where attack signals have accumulated but the evidence is not yet conclusive. In this zone, SafeDream activates contrastive imagination (Section 3.3) to proactively resolve the ambiguity.

3.3 Contrastive Imagination for Early Attack Detection

When CUSUM enters the gray zone, instead of waiting for more turns, SafeDream leverages the world model (Section 3.1) to imagine what would happen next. We first construct two action pools from the training data: an attack pool 𝒜atk\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}} containing encoded attack utterances and a benign pool 𝒜ben\mathcal{A}_{\text{ben}} containing encoded benign utterances. For each condition γ∈{atk,ben}\gamma\in\{\text{atk},\text{ben}\}, we randomly sample actions from the corresponding pool to simulate different futures. Specifically, we roll out M=8M{=}8 trajectories of H=3H{=}3 steps from the current state, autoregressively sampling actions, predicting states via gθg_{\theta}, scoring via dωd_{\omega}, and accumulating the imagined CUSUM (full procedure in Appendix A.3). After the rollout, we define the vulnerability score VtV_{t}, which compares the imagined CUSUM endpoints between attack and benign futures:

Vt=1M​∑k=1MG^t+H(k,atk)−1M​∑k=1MG^t+H(k,ben).V_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\hat{G}_{t+H}^{(k,\text{atk})}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\hat{G}_{t+H}^{(k,\text{ben})}. (6)

When VtV_{t} exceeds a threshold AimagA_{\text{imag}}, SafeDream triggers an early alarm. The rationale is: if the conversation is genuinely vulnerable, attack futures cause the imagined CUSUM to spike while benign futures keep it stable, producing a large VtV_{t}. If the conversation is safe, both futures produce similar outcomes (small gap). Empirically, we find that this contrastive design avoids the false alarms that attack-only imagination would produce (Section 4.3).

The full decision rule combines CUSUM and imagination:

Alarm​(t)={1if ​Gt≥A,1if ​τ​A<Gt<A​ and ​Vt≥Aimag,0otherwise.\text{Alarm}(t)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }G_{t}\geq A,\\ 1&\text{if }\tau A<G_{t}<A\;\text{ and }\;V_{t}\geq A_{\text{imag}},\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (7)

Imagination is triggered in gray zone, adding sub-100 ms overhead only when needed.

Fig. 3 illustrates the detection pipeline. In the gray zone, contrastive imagination forks the current state into attack and benign futures (dashed lines); the gap VtV_{t} between them determines proactive alarm (star marker) before GtG_{t} reaches AA. Conversations that skip the gray zone trigger a direct alarm (cross marker) when Gt≥AG_{t}\geq A. Benign conversations may enter the gray zone, but imagination reveals a small VtV_{t}, suppressing false alarms.

3.4 Training

Labeling.

We obtain turn-level safety labels through majority voting of three independent classifiers: HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), and MD-Judge (Li et al., 2024). The compliance point cc is the earliest turn at which a majority of the three classifiers flag the response as harmful (ℓt≥0.67\ell_{t}\geq 0.67), ensuring that the same threshold governs both training and evaluation. None of these classifiers appears as an evaluation baseline.

Loss function.

To enable smooth supervision, we use a soft label ℓt=#⁡{classifiers flagging harmful}/3\ell_{t}=\#\{\text{classifiers flagging harmful}\}/3. The total loss combines three terms:

minθ,ϕ,ω⁡ℒtrans+λ1​ℒdisc+λ2​ℒimag,\min_{\theta,\phi,\omega}\;\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{trans}}+\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{disc}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{imag}}, (8)

where ℒdisc=∑n,tBCE⁡(dω​(𝐳t(n)),ℓt(n))\mathcal{L}_{\text{disc}}=\sum_{n,t}\mathrm{BCE}(d_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(n)}),\ell_{t}^{(n)}) trains the discriminator on soft labels, ℒtrans=∑n,t‖𝐳^t(n)−sg⁡(𝐳t(n))‖22\mathcal{L}_{\text{trans}}=\sum_{n,t}\|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{(n)}-\mathrm{sg}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(n)})\|_{2}^{2} trains the transition model to predict future safety state, and ℒimag\mathcal{L}_{\text{imag}} bridges the observed-vs-imagined distribution gap by training dωd_{\omega} on imagined trajectories following DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025). The imagination loss uses a margin term to ensure separation between attack and benign risk scores, plus a calibration term to anchor absolute values (details in Appendix A.5). We set λ1=1.0\lambda_{1}=1.0, λ2=0.5\lambda_{2}=0.5.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate on three multi-turn jailbreak benchmarks that cover complementary attack characteristics. XGuard-Train (Rahman et al., 2025) (30K conversations, 13 risk categories, adaptive multi-agent attacks) serves as our primary benchmark due to its scale and diversity. SafeDialBench (Cao et al., 2025) (4K conversations, 7 distinct attack strategies, bilingual) tests generalization across diverse attack tactics. SafeMTData (Ren et al., 2025) (1.7K conversations, actor-network attacks, ∼\sim8.7 turns) provides backward compatibility with prior work such as TARS. For each benchmark, to prevent the model from learning the topic shortcuts for detection, we construct topic-matched benign contrasts to force models to distinguish based on trajectory dynamics rather than topic.

Baselines.

We compare against 8 baselines spanning two categories (full descriptions in Appendix B.2):

  • •

    Guardrail methods: WildGuard (Han et al., 2024), R2-Guard (Kang and Li, 2025), BingoGuard (Yin et al., 2025), GuardReasoner (Liu et al., 2025), SelfDefend (Wang et al., 2025) — external classifiers that evaluate each turn independently.

  • •

    Alignment-based methods: Circuit Breaker (Zou et al., 2024), X-Boundary (Lu et al., 2025), TARS (Kim et al., 2025) — methods that modify LLM weights to internalize safety.

Metrics.

We report standard detection quality metrics: Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC), Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC), F1 score, Recall, and False Positive Rate (FPR). For detection timeliness, we use Lead (detection lead time), the metric we proposed in Section 2, which measures the number of turns by which the alarm precedes the compliance point. Positive Lead indicates proactive early detection; negative Lead indicates reactive post-hoc detection. Detailed metric definitions are in Appendix B.3.

Implementation.

We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) as the frozen target LLM, following TARS (Kim et al., 2025) which also uses the Qwen2.5 family. The compliance point is defined as the first turn where a majority (at least two of three) of the consensus classifiers flag the response as harmful (ℓt≥0.67\ell_{t}\geq 0.67), matching the threshold used during training (see Appendix B.3 for justification and sensitivity analysis). All results are mean over 5-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameter selection and training details are in Appendix A.5.

4.2 Main Results

We evaluate whether SafeDream achieves earlier detection than existing methods while maintaining competitive detection quality. Table 1 presents key metrics across all three benchmarks (full results with all metrics in Appendix C.1).

Detection timeliness.

SafeDream achieves the largest detection lead across all three benchmarks: 1.11 turns on XGuard-Train, 1.20 on SafeDialBench, and 1.06 on SafeMTData. This means SafeDream warns more than one full turn before the LLM complies with the jailbreak. In contrast, all guardrail methods produce negative Lead values (e.g., WildGuard: −0.53-0.53 on XGuard-Train), detecting attacks only after the LLM has already generated harmful content. Even the strongest alignment-based method, TARS, achieves only 0.38 Lead on XGuard-Train, detecting less than half a turn before compliance.

Detection quality.

Despite being a purely external module with no LLM weight modification, SafeDream achieves the highest AUROC (0.908) on XGuard-Train, outperforming TARS (0.895) which requires full weight access. SafeDream maintains an FPR of 7.9%, substantially lower than guardrail methods (e.g., WildGuard: 22.4%) and competitive with alignment-based methods (TARS: 5.9%), which benefit from directly modifying the model’s refusal behavior. This low false positive rate is critical for deployment: a safety monitor that frequently interrupts benign conversations is impractical.

Generalization.

The advantage is consistent across benchmarks with different attack strategies. On SafeDialBench (7 distinct attack strategies, bilingual), SafeDream achieves 0.912 AUROC and 1.20 Lead, outperforming the second-best method TARS (0.865 / 0.55). On SafeMTData (actor-network attacks), SafeDream achieves 0.915 AUROC and 1.06 Lead versus TARS’s 0.847 / 0.31.

4.3 Ablation Studies

To understand the contribution of each component, we systematically remove one module at a time and measure the impact on detection quality and timeliness (Table 2).

  • •

    Imagination enables early detection. Removing imagination (Section 3.3) drops Lead from 1.11 to 0.53, confirming that imagination is the key of proactive early detection.

  • •

    CUSUM enables low false alarm rate. Removing CUSUM (Section 3.2) increases Lead to 1.49, however, FPR surges to 13.8%, indicating that CUSUM is essential for suppressing false alarms.

  • •

    Concept cone grounds the latent space. Removing the concept cone (Section 3.1) causes the most severe overall degradation (F1: 0.891→\to0.740, FPR: 7.9%→\to15.5%), indicating that the cone projection encodes essential safety-relevant knowledge.

  • •

    Transition model enables dynamics. Removing the transition model (Section 3.1) drops Lead to 0.30 and F1 to 0.775, as the system loses both imagination capability and multi-turn state integration and reduces to single-turn classification.

  • •

    Contrastive design calibrates imagination. Attack-only imagination (Section 3.3) reduces Lead from 1.11 to 1.01 and increases FPR from 7.9% to 25.6%, confirming that comparing against benign futures is necessary to avoid overestimating vulnerability.

We further sweep the imagination hyperparameters (HH, MM) and concept cone dimensionality (KK). Fig. 4 shows that H=3H{=}3 and M=8M{=}8 maximize Lead, with diminishing returns beyond these values, while the full 5-dim cone consistently outperforms lower-dimensional projections. Additional ablations (transition model architecture) are in Appendix C.3.

5 Related Work

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks and countermeasures.

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks (Russinovich et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026) achieve >>90% ASR by distributing malicious intent across seemingly innocuous turns. To counter these threats, guardrail methods (Han et al., 2024; Kang and Li, 2025; Yin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) deploy external classifiers, while alignment-based methods (Zou et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025) modify LLM weights to internalize safety. Like these methods, SafeDream also aims to detect and prevent jailbreaks. However, guardrails evaluate each turn independently and cannot model the cumulative safety degradation that multi-turn attacks exploit; alignment-based methods require retraining, precluding deployment on closed-source models. Most critically, both paradigms are reactive: they detect harmful content only after it manifests. SafeDream addresses all three issues: it operates as an external module (no weight modification), models multi-turn dynamics (not per-turn classification), and detects attacks before the LLM complies (proactive rather than reactive).

Safety representations and world models.

Arditi et al. (2024) discover a refusal direction in LLM hidden states; RDO (Wollschläger et al., 2025) extends this to a multi-dimensional concept cone; SRR (Du et al., 2025) and ReGA (Wei et al., 2025) leverage internal representations for safety ranking and runtime safeguarding. SafeDream shares with these methods the insight that LLM hidden states encode rich safety-relevant geometric structure. However, prior work treats these representations as static features for single-turn classification or analysis, without modeling how they evolve during a multi-turn conversation. SafeDream addresses this gap by learning a transition model over safety states, enabling prediction of future safety trajectories. This dynamics-based approach draws on world models from RL (Hafner et al., 2025; Teoh et al., 2025), which learn environment dynamics and use imagined rollouts to evaluate futures without real interaction. While world models are typically used for planning (selecting optimal actions), SafeDream adapts them for detection: imagining both attack and benign futures to assess whether a conversation is heading toward jailbreak compliance, thus achieves proactive warning with low FPR.

6 Conclusion

We proposed SafeDream, a lightweight external module that requires no LLM weight modification. SafeDream formulates the proactive early jailbreak detection problem and introduces a new metric, detection lead, to measure detection timeliness. It combines a safety state world model for future state prediction, CUSUM for multi-turn evidence accumulation, and contrastive imagination for proactive early warning. On three benchmarks against 8 baselines, SafeDream achieves the best detection timeliness (1.06–1.20 turns before compliance) while maintaining competitive false positive rates, outperforming all baselines in detection quality. Ablation studies confirm that each component is effective: contrastive imagination drives early detection, CUSUM suppresses false alarms, and the concept cone grounds the safety latent space. Limitations are discussed in Appendix D.

Appendix A Method Details

A.1 Notation Summary

Table 3 summarizes all notation used in this paper.

A.2 Architecture Details

Why Transformer over RNN.

Multi-turn attack strategies involve long-range dependencies: gradual escalation, strategy switching, and topic drift span many turns. The self-attention mechanism naturally captures dependencies between arbitrary turn pairs. Teoh et al. (2025) confirm that Transformers can learn compact latent world models effectively.

Layer selection.

We select layer 19 by running the Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) algorithm (Wollschläger et al., 2025) on harmful and harmless prompts from SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024), sweeping over layers and selecting the one that yields the highest refusal manipulation effectiveness for Qwen2.5-7B. This layer choice is model- and scale-specific and must be re-determined for other architectures.

Cross-attention details.

The safety signature 𝐬t∈ℝ5\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} (detached from the computation graph) is linearly projected to produce query vectors Q=WQ​𝐬tQ=W_{Q}\mathbf{s}_{t}. The full hidden state 𝐡t∈ℝ3584\mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3584} is partitioned into a sequence of fixed-size chunks, and each chunk is linearly projected to produce keys KK and values VV. Standard cross-attention retrieves the most relevant features: XAttnϕ​(𝐬t,𝐡t)=softmax​(Q​K⊤/dk)​V∈ℝdext\text{XAttn}_{\phi}(\mathbf{s}_{t},\mathbf{h}_{t})=\text{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}})V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ext}}}.

Transition model details.

The Transformer gθg_{\theta} has 4 layers, 4 attention heads, model dimension 128, and Pre-LN normalization. Since 𝐳t∈ℝ69\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{69} and 𝐚t∈ℝ64\mathbf{a}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} are concatenated, a linear layer projects the 133-dimensional input to the internal dimension of 128; output tokens are projected back to 69 dimensions.

A.3 Imagination Procedure Details

Action pool construction.

The attack pool 𝒜atk\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}} and benign pool 𝒜ben\mathcal{A}_{\text{ben}} are constructed from the training fold of each cross-validation split. We encode every user turn from attack conversations as 𝐚t=ψ⁡(ut)\mathbf{a}_{t}=\psi(u_{t}) and collect them into 𝒜atk\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}}; likewise, all user turns from benign conversations form 𝒜ben\mathcal{A}_{\text{ben}}. All turns are included regardless of their position in the conversation (i.e., both early benign-looking turns and late escalation turns from attack conversations enter 𝒜atk\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}}). We use uniform random sampling from these pools during imagination. Importantly, the pools are reconstructed for each cross-validation fold using only training data, ensuring no test-fold leakage. The pool operates entirely in the 64-dimensional action embedding space, so imagination does not require decoding back to text or invoking the LLM.

Rollout procedure.

For each condition γ∈{atk,ben}\gamma\in\{\text{atk},\text{ben}\}, we roll out M=8M{=}8 independent trajectories of horizon H=3H{=}3, each initialized from the current observed state (𝐳^t(k,γ)=𝐳t\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{(k,\gamma)}=\mathbf{z}_{t}, G^t(k,γ)=Gt\hat{G}_{t}^{(k,\gamma)}=G_{t}). At each imagined step j=1,…,Hj=1,\ldots,H, we sample an action 𝐚t+j(k,γ)∼𝒜γ\mathbf{a}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)}\sim\mathcal{A}_{\gamma} uniformly at random, predict the next safety state:

𝐳^t+j(k,γ)=gθ​((𝐳0,𝐚1),…,(𝐳t−1,𝐚t)⏟real context,(𝐳^t(k,γ),𝐚t+1(k,γ)),…,(𝐳^t+j−1(k,γ),𝐚t+j(k,γ))⏟imagined context),\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)}=g_{\theta}\!\big(\underbrace{(\mathbf{z}_{0},\mathbf{a}_{1}),\ldots,(\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\mathbf{a}_{t})}_{\text{real context}},\;\underbrace{(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{(k,\gamma)},\mathbf{a}_{t+1}^{(k,\gamma)}),\ldots,(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+j-1}^{(k,\gamma)},\mathbf{a}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)})}_{\text{imagined context}}\big), (9)

score it via r^t+j(k,γ)=dω​(𝐳^t+j(k,γ))\hat{r}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)}=d_{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)}), and update the imagined CUSUM:

G^t+j(k,γ)=max⁡(0,G^t+j−1(k,γ)+logitϵ​(r^t+j(k,γ))−κ).\hat{G}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)}=\max\!\big(0,\;\hat{G}_{t+j-1}^{(k,\gamma)}+\mathrm{logit}_{\epsilon}(\hat{r}_{t+j}^{(k,\gamma)})-\kappa\big). (10)

A.4 Imagination Loss Details

The imagination loss encourages the discriminator to separate attack from benign imagined states:

ℒimag=max⁡(0,δ−(ratk−rben))⏟margin+λcal​[BCE⁡(ratk,1)+BCE⁡(rben,0)]⏟calibration,\mathcal{L}_{\text{imag}}=\underbrace{\max\!\big(0,\;\delta-(r_{\text{atk}}-r_{\text{ben}})\big)}_{\text{margin}}+\lambda_{\text{cal}}\underbrace{\big[\mathrm{BCE}(r_{\text{atk}},1)+\mathrm{BCE}(r_{\text{ben}},0)\big]}_{\text{calibration}}, (11)

where ratk=dω​(sg⁡(𝐳^t+Hatk))r_{\text{atk}}=d_{\omega}(\mathrm{sg}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+H}^{\text{atk}})), rben=dω​(sg⁡(𝐳^t+Hben))r_{\text{ben}}=d_{\omega}(\mathrm{sg}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+H}^{\text{ben}})), δ=0.3\delta=0.3, and λcal=0.5\lambda_{\text{cal}}=0.5. The margin term ensures a clear gap between attack and benign risk scores (directly determining VtV_{t}), while the calibration term anchors absolute values to prevent degenerate solutions where both scores are high (false alarms) or both low (missed detections).

A.5 Training Configuration

We use AdamW with learning rate 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, batch size 128, up to 200 epochs with 5-fold cross-validation and early stopping (patience 20 on validation safety loss). Gradient clipping is set to 1.0. We use CosineAnnealing learning rate scheduling with Tmax=200T_{\max}=200. Loss weights: λ1=1.0\lambda_{1}=1.0 (discrimination), λ2=0.5\lambda_{2}=0.5 (imagination). The margin in ℒimag\mathcal{L}_{\text{imag}} is δ=0.3\delta=0.3 with calibration weight λcal=0.5\lambda_{\text{cal}}=0.5.

Gradient routing.

The cone projections (𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t}) are hardcoded with no gradient. The transition model θ\theta receives gradients from ℒtrans\mathcal{L}_{\text{trans}} only; input states 𝐳t−1\mathbf{z}_{t-1} are detached so gradients do not flow back into ϕ\phi. The cross-attention parameters ϕ\phi are updated through ℒdisc\mathcal{L}_{\text{disc}} via dω​(𝐳t)d_{\omega}(\mathbf{z}_{t}), since 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} depends on XAttnϕ\text{XAttn}_{\phi}. The discriminator ω\omega receives gradients from both ℒdisc\mathcal{L}_{\text{disc}} and ℒimag\mathcal{L}_{\text{imag}}; imagined states are stop-gradiented, making ω\omega the only parameter updated by the imagination loss.

Appendix B Full Experimental Setup

B.1 Dataset Statistics

We use XGuard-Train (Rahman et al., 2025) as our primary evaluation dataset. XGuard-Train contains 30,695 multi-turn jailbreak conversations spanning 13 risk categories, generated via the X-Teaming multi-agent framework with diverse attack strategies. The average dialogue length is around 5 turns.

Topic-matched benign construction.

For each attack dialogue, we extract the topic from the first user turn and prompt GPT-4o to generate a multi-turn benign conversation on the same topic with a similar number of turns. To ensure quality, we verify with all three labeling classifiers (HarmBench, GPT-4o, MD-Judge) that no turn in the generated benign conversation is flagged as harmful; any flagged conversation is regenerated. This topic-matching procedure ensures that the only distinguishing signal between attack and benign conversations is the trajectory dynamics (gradual safety erosion), not the surface-level topic. We apply the same procedure to all three benchmarks (XGuard-Train, SafeDialBench, SafeMTData).

B.2 Baseline Descriptions

We compare against two categories of baselines:

Guardrail methods (5): WildGuard (Han et al., 2024), R2-Guard (Kang and Li, 2025), BingoGuard (Yin et al., 2025), GuardReasoner (Liu et al., 2025), and SelfDefend (Wang et al., 2025).

Alignment-based methods (3): Circuit Breaker (Zou et al., 2024), X-Boundary (Lu et al., 2025), and TARS (Kim et al., 2025).

Detection protocol for alignment-based methods.

Alignment-based methods (Circuit Breaker, X-Boundary, TARS) modify LLM weights to resist attacks rather than producing explicit detection signals. To evaluate them as detectors under our unified protocol, we define detection as follows: at each turn tt, we feed the conversation prefix oto_{t} to the alignment-modified LLM and check whether its response constitutes a refusal (using the refusal detection task of WildGuard (Han et al., 2024)). If the alignment-modified LLM refuses at turn tt, we record tt as the detection turn tdett^{\text{det}}. If the model complies (produces non-refusal content), the turn is not flagged. For computing a continuous risk score (needed for AUROC/AUPRC), we use the refusal probability from the alignment-modified LLM’s output logits where available, or the WildGuard refusal confidence score otherwise. Note that this protocol gives alignment-based methods a natural advantage on FPR: because they directly modify the model’s refusal behavior, they rarely refuse benign conversations, yielding inherently low false positive rates. This explains why TARS achieves the lowest FPR in our evaluation despite being designed for safety alignment rather than detection.

Detection protocol for guardrail methods.

Each guardrail evaluates the user prompt and/or LLM response at every turn independently. We use each guardrail’s default prompt template and harmfulness task configuration. A turn is flagged as harmful if the guardrail’s output exceeds its default decision threshold. The detection turn tdett^{\text{det}} is the first flagged turn in the conversation. For AUROC/AUPRC computation, we use each guardrail’s continuous confidence score (probability or logit) as the per-conversation risk score, taking the maximum across all turns. Since guardrails evaluate each turn independently without modeling multi-turn dynamics, they can only detect attacks after harmful content manifests, resulting in negative Lead values.

Guardrail model versions.

WildGuard: allenai/wildguard (7B, response harmfulness task). R2-Guard: official implementation with MLN reasoning (Kang and Li, 2025). BingoGuard: llama3.1-8B variant, 5-level severity grading (levels ≥\geq3 counted as harmful) (Yin et al., 2025). GuardReasoner: 8B model with chain-of-thought reasoning enabled (Liu et al., 2025). SelfDefend: fine-tuned Llama-2-7B with dual-prompt pipeline (P_direct + P_intent) (Wang et al., 2025).

Alignment-based model training on Qwen2.5-7B.

All alignment-based methods were retrained on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct following each method’s official training procedure and publicly released code: Circuit Breaker uses representation rerouting with the retain set from Zou et al. (2024) adapted to Qwen’s layer structure. X-Boundary follows the official code release with both single-turn and multi-turn safety training data (Lu et al., 2025). TARS uses the λ=0.5\lambda{=}0.5 harmful/harmless reward mixture with GRPO on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (Kim et al., 2025).

Labeling classifier details.

Turn-level labels are produced by HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) (fine-tuned Llama-2-13B classifier), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), and MD-Judge (Li et al., 2024) (fine-tuned Mistral-7B). Each classifier receives only the LLM’s response text for the current turn (without conversation history) to ensure per-turn independence.

B.3 Metric Definitions

  • •

    Lead (Detection Lead Time): Lead=1|𝒟atk|​∑i(ci−tidet)\text{Lead}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{atk}}|}\sum_{i}(c_{i}-t_{i}^{\text{det}}). Higher is better; negative values indicate detection after compliance.

  • •

    EWR (Early Warning Rate): fraction of attack dialogues where SafeDream detects earlier than the baseline.

Compliance point and label design.

Defining what constitutes a “successful” jailbreak—and at which turn it occurs—is a recognized open problem. Ran et al. (2024) document that “there is surprisingly no consensus on how to evaluate whether a jailbreak attempt is successful.” Existing approaches span a wide spectrum: conversation-level binary (Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2025): at least one turn flagged by a judge), final-turn outcome (TROJail: reward on last response only), per-turn binary (HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024): classify each response independently), and multi-turn escalation (Siege (Zhou, 2025): tree-search-based multi-turn attacks that exploit partial compliance accumulating across turns). Siege demonstrates that minor concessions can be systematically exploited to eventually obtain disallowed content.

We adopt a unified labeling framework based on a consensus of three safety classifiers—HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), and MD-Judge (Li et al., 2024)—each evaluating every response independently. The graduated label averages their outputs and serves both as the training signal for the safety discriminator and as the basis for the compliance point definition:

  • •

    Training: the graduated labels ℓt\ell_{t} capture progressive safety degradation, providing the discriminator with a smooth signal that reflects escalation dynamics rather than a sharp binary transition.

  • •

    Evaluation: the compliance point cc is defined as the first turn at which ℓt≥0.67\ell_{t}\geq 0.67 (a majority of classifiers flag the response as harmful). Detection Lead is then Lead=c−tdet\text{Lead}=c-t^{\text{det}}. Using the same threshold for training and evaluation ensures consistency: the model is trained to detect turns that the evaluation deems harmful.

This unified design ensures that training and evaluation operate on the same notion of safety degradation. None of these three classifiers appears as an evaluation baseline in Table 1, ensuring complete separation between label sources and evaluation targets.

All metrics are averaged over 5 folds. Table 4 reports standard deviations for key metrics on XGuard-Train; all differences between SafeDream and baselines are statistically significant (p<0.01p<0.01, paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples).

Sensitivity to compliance threshold θ\theta.

Our primary results use θ=0.67\theta=0.67 (majority vote) to define the compliance point. To verify that our conclusions are robust to this choice, Table 5 reports Lead for SafeDream and the strongest baselines across a range of thresholds on XGuard-Train. A lower θ\theta (e.g., 0.33) places the compliance point earlier, reducing Lead for all methods; a higher θ\theta (e.g., 1.0) places it later, inflating Lead. Crucially, SafeDream maintains the largest Lead at every threshold, confirming that the advantage is not an artifact of the chosen θ\theta.

Appendix C Extended Results

C.1 Full Benchmark Results

Table 6, Table 7, and Table 8 present the complete results with all metrics on the three benchmarks.

C.2 Imagination and Cone Hyperparameters

The hyperparameter sensitivity for imagination horizon HH, trajectory count MM, and concept cone dimensionality KK is visualized in Fig. 4 (main text). H=3H{=}3 maximizes both F1 and Lead; M=8M{=}8 saturates the benefit; the full 5-dim cone (K=5K{=}5) consistently outperforms lower-dimensional projections. K=1K{=}1 reduces to the single refusal direction of Arditi et al. (Arditi et al., 2024).

C.3 Transition Model Architecture

We compare three architectures for the transition model on attack-vs-benign trajectory classification (Table 9) using topic-matched benign contrasts that force models to rely on temporal dynamics rather than topic shortcuts.

The Transformer achieves the highest AUROC (0.908) and shows the largest sensitivity to turn order (Δ\DeltaAUROC = 0.275): shuffling the turn order causes a 27.5% drop, confirming that the model relies on temporal structure rather than bag-of-turns features. The MLP, which processes each turn independently, performs near chance (0.517), demonstrating that per-turn features alone are insufficient for multi-turn attack detection. This validates our choice of a Transformer-based transition model.

C.4 Computational Overhead

SafeDream adds minimal latency: the Safety-State Transformer forward pass takes <<5ms per turn, and contrastive imagination (when triggered) adds <<100ms. The module occupies negligible GPU memory alongside the frozen 7B LLM.

Appendix D Limitations

SafeDream requires access to the frozen LLM’s intermediate representations (layer 19 hidden states), limiting deployment to settings where hidden states are accessible. The concept cone geometry is model-family-specific and must be re-extracted for each target LLM; validating the anchoring across diverse model families remains future work. The transition model learns dynamics from specific attack strategies observed during training; zero-shot transfer to entirely unseen attack families may require retraining. The contrastive imagination samples actions i.i.d. per step from the action pools, while real attacks may exhibit strategic correlations that the i.i.d. assumption could underestimate. Additionally, our evaluation relies on three specific safety classifiers to define ground-truth compliance points; disagreements among classifiers or blind spots shared by all three could introduce systematic labeling bias. Finally, while we evaluate on three diverse benchmarks, all experiments use a single target LLM (Qwen2.5-7B); extending to other model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) requires validating and re-extracting the concept cone geometry and retraining the transition model, though the lightweight architecture makes this practical.
